newsitem.title: THAILAND: FORECAST-Thai market focus swings to reserves data.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Thai market focus swings to reserves data.

text.p: Thailand's bleak economic landscape, particularly its faltering foreign reserves, will be the focus for financial markets this week when the central bank releases key monthly data, analysts said on Tuesday.

They expect to see another deficit in the balance of payments for May, while foreign reserves are likely to shrink further after last month's speculative attack on the embattled baht and subsequent intervention.

Seasonal factors are expected to push Thailand's trade deficit to between 26 billion baht and 30 billion baht ($1.04 billion-$1.2 billion) in April from 22.2 billion baht in March, despite positive year-on-year growth in exports.
"The overall picture will remain one of doom and gloom," said Phillip Smyth, regional economist at Asia Equity.

"But April is always a bad month for trade ... year-on-year growth will be around 8.8 percent but the month-on-month figure will be down by 10.2 percent," he added. April is traditionally a long holiday season for Thais.

On Thursday the Bank of Thailand releases its latest leading monthly economic indicators. These cover foreign reserves, balance of payments, and money supply for May along with trade figures, the current account balance and the private investment index for April.

Economists' estimates of May foreign reserves ranged from $30 billion to $36 billion, a substantial drop from April's $37.3 billion. But they differed widely in their interpretations of the falls in the reserves.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, said investors should not be alarmed by the slide in reserves and the drop should bottom out soon.
"Objectively, it should not be the level that should induce panic over the Thai baht. But of course, the trend might cause some concerns on where it will bottom out," he said.

"Capital controls imposed last month on the Thai baht suggest that it will bottom out soon because the (baht) attack has probably subsided. Unwinding of forward cover (positions on the baht) might not be severe from now on," Song said.

The central bank imposed controls after the last attack on the baht, cutting supplies to foreign speculators from local sources. The move created a two-tier baht market -- one offshore and another domestic.
With a drop in imports, the ratio between foreign reserves and imports was likely to remain unchanged, Song added. Foreign reserves are normally measured by the equivalent value of months of imports.

But Supavudh Saicheua, a vice president at Phatra Thanakit Plc, forecast a drop in reserves to $30-34 billion and said concerns about the fall were justified given the country's foreign debt situation and tight local liquidity.
"It's no longer relevant to link foreign reserves to imports. Reserves are more related now to (the amount of) foreign debt and ... domestic money supply," he said.
At the end of May, Thailand had $85 billion in foreign debt. Of this $66 billion was owed by the private sector, and mostly borrowed through facilities with maturities of a year or less.

With Thailand running a balance of payments deficit so far this year, some analysts fear the country could be forced to use its shrinking foreign reserves to repay the debts, a move that could hurt its ability to defend the baht.
